# Publish Many {#sec-publish-many}

```{python}
#| label: ch14-setup
from scripts import water as w
from scripts.prose import number_words, text_holds

s = w.res()["summary"]
k = s["k"]
```

```{python}
#| label: ch14-rebuild
# The rebuild in the summary, computed: the finished analysis again with MAX_MISSING = 1 instead
# of its setting, in memory, as in @sec-answer-water; then where Tunja's zones and the department
# capitals' rural zones went.
from pathlib import Path


NUM = number_words(zero="no")


A = w.A
before = w.res()
original = A.MAX_MISSING
A.MAX_MISSING = 1
try:
    after = A.run()
finally:
    A.MAX_MISSING = original
c0, c1 = before["clusters"], after["clusters"]
cap0 = c0[(c0["department_capital"] == 1) & (c0["zone"] == "rural")]
cap1 = c1[(c1["department_capital"] == 1) & (c1["zone"] == "rural")]
tj0, tj1 = c0[c0["divipola"] == "15001"], c1[c1["divipola"] == "15001"]
tj_rural0 = int((tj0["zone"] == "rural").sum())
tj_c = int(tj0["cluster"].iloc[0])
kept = c0.merge(c1, on=["divipola", "zone", "year"], suffixes=("_0", "_1"))
same = (kept["cluster_0"] == kept["cluster_1"]).mean()
# The rows the stricter rule drops, which reach it with coverage missing (imputation comes after).
gone = c0.merge(c1[["divipola", "zone", "year"]], on=["divipola", "zone", "year"], how="left", indicator=True)
gone = gone[gone["_merge"] == "left_only"]
gone_cap = (gone["department_capital"] == 1) & (gone["zone"] == "rural")
gone_both = gone[["water_coverage_imputed", "sewer_coverage_imputed"]].eq(1).all(axis=1)
other_both = int((gone_both & ~gone_cap).sum())
text_holds(gone_both.all() and gone_cap.sum() == len(cap0) and len(gone) == len(c0) - len(c1),
           "what the stricter rule drops")
text_holds(original == 2 and len(cap1) == 0 and len(cap0) > 0
           and cap0[["water_coverage_imputed", "sewer_coverage_imputed"]].eq(1).all().all()
           and set(tj1["zone"]) == {"urban"} and tj1["cluster"].eq(tj_c).all()
           and len(tj1) == (tj0["zone"] == "urban").sum() and tj0["cluster"].eq(tj_c).all()
           and after["k"] == before["k"] == 4    # the post's `assert k == 4`
           and list(after["profiles"]["name"]) == list(before["profiles"]["name"]),
           "the MAX_MISSING rebuild")
geo_mb = Path("../examples/water/data/municipios.geojson").stat().st_size / 1e6
```

The officials will read the findings as a report, so they need it in the formats offices pass around:
Word and PDF. The municipal council will see them on a screen in a meeting, and will look to the last
slide for the conclusion. Both will look for where to act, and anyone else needs a link. So the project
gets a report, slides, and a website with a blog post, and not one of them may compute anything. Each
reads `outputs/`, and that is what makes the chapter's last test fair: change one setting in the
analysis, predict what follows, rebuild, and check that every publication followed. On the way, the old
trade-off between recomputing and caching comes back, now that the project is big enough for it to
matter.

## The report, in Word and PDF {#sec-water-report}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Create report.qmd (formats html, docx, typst) from outputs/: summary, question, data (IRCA = utility-supplied prestadores IRCA), method, heatmap, outcomes, correlation ≠ causation (a chart of median infant_mortality by IRCA band per cluster), limits, sources. Matplotlib figures with captions and alt text; hide code. Render all formats; report errors.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
writes `report.qmd` · `uv run quarto render report.qmd`
:::

::: {.you}
open `report.docx` (Word or LibreOffice) and `report.pdf`
:::

The prompt lists the report's sections, and three of its choices carry the lessons of the last chapters.
"Utility-supplied" is in the data section because @sec-water-why showed what the label hides.
"Correlation ≠ causation" is a section, not a footnote. And the figures are matplotlib, because Word,
PowerPoint and PDF cannot run the JavaScript that interactive Plotly charts need (@fig-water-report).

## The report as an e-book (optional) {#sec-water-epub}

::: {.prompt}
```default
In report.qmd, add an epub format (toc: true), set lang: en, and add ePub to the html `format-links`. Render report.qmd and check that report.epub contains the three figures and the sources.
```
:::

An EPUB is a zipped set of web pages whose text reflows to fit the reader's screen. Most e-book readers
do not run JavaScript, so figures must be static images, which the report's already are. `lang: en`
records the book's language (without it the file declares an unknown one), and `toc: true` adds a
table of contents. Open the result in Apple Books on a Mac or in Calibre.

The book in your hands is the same thing at a larger scale, and building it showed where a report-sized
EPUB stops being enough. Parts and part pages disappear from a Quarto book's EPUB; content marked for
HTML also appears in EPUB unless it is marked for HTML with JavaScript; Quarto's built-in callout and code
colours vanish on a reader's night theme; and an EPUB checker rejects markup that every browser accepts.
@sec-how-built describes each problem and its fix.

## A website with a blog {#sec-water-website}

The publications become one website, with a blog post that tells the story in prose:

```yaml
# _quarto.yml
project:
  type: website
  execute-dir: project               # <1>
  pre-render: scripts/analysis.py    # <2>
execute:
  freeze: false                      # <3>
```
1. Every page, including a post in `posts/…/`, reads `outputs/` and `data/` from the project folder.
2. Quarto runs the analysis before every render, including a single page's render: `outputs/` is always
   fresh.
3. Every render re-executes every page, so every page shows the outputs just written.

```yaml
# index.qmd
listing:
  contents: posts                    # <1>
```
1. A *listing* turns every `posts/*/index.qmd` into an entry on the home page: a blog.

::: {.prompt}
```default
Make this folder a Quarto website: _quarto.yml (execute-dir: project, `pre-render` scripts/analysis.py, freeze: false, render list, navbar), index.qmd listing posts/, and one post titled with the real k, e.g. "Four kinds of municipal zone". Render it; check the links.
```
:::

::: {.you}
`uv run quarto preview`
:::

The post's title states the number of clusters, so a change in the analysis could leave it wrong. The
finished post protects itself with one line in its setup cell, `assert k == 4`, which fails the render if
the analysis ever finds a different k. A loud failure is better than a quiet falsehood
(@fig-water-post).

![The finished blog post, whose title states the number of clusters the analysis found. Rendered from `examples/water/posts/four-kinds-of-municipal-zone/index.qmd`.](../media/figures/water-post.png){#fig-water-post width=85% fig-alt="A blog post titled Four kinds of municipal zone, tagged water, clustering and Colombia, with an opening paragraph about the zone-years and the nine features used, and a list of the four kinds, each with its zone-years, municipalities, median IRCA, piped-water coverage and poverty."}

### Fresh or frozen?

`freeze: false` is the simple, safe setting: every render recomputes everything, so nothing can be stale.
The cost is time, every render, for every page. `freeze: auto` is the alternative: Quarto stores each
page's results in `_freeze/` and re-executes a page only when *its own source* changes.

The catch is in that last phrase. Quarto does not know which files a page reads, so a change to `data/` or
to `outputs/` is not detected, and a frozen page keeps its old numbers. With `freeze: auto` you need a rule
for throwing results away: delete `_freeze/` (or render that one page directly, which ignores the cache)
whenever the data or the analysis change.

::: practice
Start with `freeze: false` and switch only when renders become slow enough to matter, and when you do,
write the invalidation rule down where the next person will find it. This book uses `freeze: auto`, so the
EPUB rebuilds quickly and reproducibly, and its rule is written in its configuration and README: after any
change to the examples' data or analysis, run `make book-fresh`, which deletes `_freeze/` and re-executes
every chapter.
:::

## Publish it {#sec-water-ship}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Initialise a git repository here with a .gitignore for _site/, .quarto/, .venv/, outputs/ and *_files/. Replace README.md in this folder with a short one linking to https://<your-github-username>.github.io/water-quality/ and listing the files in the site's Downloads menu. Commit everything not ignored, then create a public GitHub repository named `water-quality` with gh and push to it. Set the repository's website to the same URL with `gh repo edit --homepage`. Show me the README and the website URL you set.
```
:::

::: {.you}
approve `gh` · when it shows the website URL, in the second tab: `uv run quarto publish gh-pages`, then Enter at "Publish site … (Y/n)" · open the live address
:::

The steps are Part II's (@sec-london-publish), with one addition to the `.gitignore`: `outputs/`, which
the pre-render step rebuilds. The data are public, and `data/README.md` lists each source's terms:
CC BY-SA 4.0 for DANE's DIVIPOLA list and the INS, ICFES and MEN tables, CC BY 4.0 for TerriData and
CHIRPS, citation terms for DANE's population and boundaries, and none for SRTM. Publishing them with the
site is fine, provided the attributions travel with them and the CC BY-SA data, and what is built from
them, such as `water_municipal.csv`, stay under that licence, as its ShareAlike condition requires
([CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/), checked 2026-11-12). In a test run on 2026-11-01 the first publish took about two minutes, then GitHub Pages built
the site in 20 to 35 seconds.

::: practice
**Pause and think**, while it publishes: what is the difference between your folder and the live site?

The live site is the last `_site/` you published. Changes in your folder, including re-rendered outputs,
do not appear online until you publish again.
:::

Build the report, the slides and the website, then publish.

and the blog post.

## Change an input, explain the rebuild {#sec-water-change}

This is the second task with no prompt supplied, and the test of this part's design.

::: tryit
1. **Predict.** In `scripts/analysis.py`, change `MAX_MISSING = 2` to `1`. Which outputs will change,
   and what will happen to Tunja's two zones?
2. **Rebuild** the site.
3. **Explain** which outputs changed, which did not, and why.
4. **Undo** the change (`git restore scripts/analysis.py`) and rebuild, so the outputs match the real
   settings.

::: done
you can name the outputs that changed, the ones that did not, and why.
:::
:::

`MAX_MISSING` drops rows missing more than that many of the nine features (@sec-prepare). A strong answer
names the mechanism: `pre-render` re-runs the analysis, which rewrites every file in `outputs/`, and
`freeze: false` re-executes every page that reads them. It checks at least two outputs against the new row
counts. And it notices what did not change, including the live site. The model answer, computed with the
setting changed, is in @sec-checkpoints, and the summary below follows Tunja through the rebuild.

## A dashboard and a white paper (optional) {#sec-water-dashboard}

A dashboard can show the clusters on a map. The first prompt builds a Plotly map of each urban zone's IRCA
band with a year slider; the second adds pages for the kinds, the outcomes and the method:

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
Create dashboard.qmd (format: dashboard): a Plotly choropleth of the IRCA band of the "urban" rows of outputs/clusters.parquet on data/municipios.geojson (featureidkey="properties.divipola"), a year slider over their years (frames update only z), an itables table of outputs/clusters.parquet (maxBytes=0); end each chart cell with `fig`. Make it polished: IRCA bands in order from no risk to unfit, light to dark, with a legend, titled cards and readable labels. Add it to the navbar; render, check it looks good at laptop size and report errors.
```
:::

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
Add Kinds, Outcomes and Method pages to dashboard.qmd from outputs/ only: a heatmap of cluster_profiles.csv's `z_` columns; outcomes_by_year.csv medians by `year` and `cluster`, and irca_infant.csv's ρ; k_selection.csv's inertia and silhouette by k. Use each cluster's `color` and axis units; say it is descriptive, not causal. Render; check each page at laptop size.
```
:::

![The finished dashboard's map page. Rendered from `examples/water/dashboard.qmd`.](../media/figures/water-dashboard.png){#fig-water-dashboard fig-alt="The dashboard's Map page: four value boxes (zone-years clustered, the number of kinds, the median urban IRCA in 2023 and the share of sampled rural zones in the high or unfit band), a map of Colombia's municipalities coloured by the IRCA band of their urban zone, light for no risk to dark for unfit, with a year slider, a table of the four kinds with their zone-years and median IRCA, and a note about the map's data. Tabs lead to the Kinds, Outcomes, Method and Municipalities pages."}

::: pitfall
Three traps, all met building the example. The boundary file follows the GeoJSON standard (exterior rings
counter-clockwise) and Plotly expects the opposite, so without reversing the rings every municipality is
drawn as "the world minus the municipality", a grey rectangle; the finished script's `load_geojson()`
reverses them. Animation frames must update only the colours (`z`): if every year repeats the
`{python} f"{geo_mb:.1f}"` MB of boundaries, the page balloons. And a dashboard cell shows every top-level expression, not only the last, so
a bare `fig.add_vline(…)` draws the chart twice; assign it, `fig = fig.add_vline(…)`, and end the cell
with `fig`. The searchable table needs `maxBytes=0`, or `itables` silently drops rows to keep the page
small.
:::

The same outputs can also become an academic paper, as London's did (@sec-london-whitepaper), now with
numbered equations (`$$ … $$ {#eq-kmeans}`, referred to as `@eq-kmeans`) and citations of the papers behind
each method:

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
Create whitepaper.qmd from outputs/: A4 Typst, "New Computer Modern"; an abstract (no inline code), numbered Introduction, Methods with equations, Results and Conclusions, then References via `#set bibliography(title: [References])`. Cite data/README.md's sources and the k-means, silhouette and ARI papers in references.bib; open each DOI. Add it to `render` and the "Downloads" menu; render; check equations and citations. Figures must be vector: set `fig-format: svg` and check that the files in `figure-typst/` end in .svg.
```
:::

::: pitfall
"Open each DOI" is there for a reason: an assistant can produce a plausible reference that does not exist.
Ask it to drop any reference it cannot open rather than guess, and check the reference list yourself. The
finished paper cites Lloyd (1982) for k-means, Rousseeuw (1987) for the silhouette, Hubert and Arabie
(1985) for the adjusted Rand index and Pedregosa et al. (2011) for scikit-learn, each checked against its
publisher's page on 2026-11-01.
:::

![The first page of the finished water white paper. Rendered from `examples/water/whitepaper.qmd`.](../media/figures/water-whitepaper-p1.png){#fig-water-whitepaper width=70% .on-light fig-alt="The first page of an A4 paper set in a LaTeX-style typeface, titled Drinking-water quality and infant mortality in Colombian municipal zones, with the subtitle A descriptive cluster analysis, 2016 to 2023, an abstract, and the start of a numbered Introduction with citations in square brackets."}

## Further challenges {#sec-water-stretch}

These have no checkpoints. Each extends the analysis with data already in the project, or names one that
is not yet available:

- **Moves between kinds.** Count how municipalities' zones move between clusters from 2016 to 2023, and
  draw it as a Sankey diagram (Plotly's `go.Sankey`).
- **Positive deviants.** Find municipalities whose rural zone is in the high-risk kind yet whose recorded
  infant mortality is low, and check first whether that is small numbers, blanks or under-registration.
- **Other clusterings.** A Gaussian mixture model gives each row a probability per cluster instead of a hard
  label; HDBSCAN finds dense groups and leaves outliers unclustered. Do the kinds survive?
- **A better outcome.** Diarrhoeal disease in children under five is the outcome most directly linked to
  water. Its incidence is not in the open SIVIGILA data, which publish only deaths; the data's README records
  it as a source to add when it becomes available.

## Summary {.unnumbered}

Part III ends on a prediction. Set `MAX_MISSING` to 1, and every row missing more than one of the nine
features goes. Department capitals have no zone-level coverage, so their rural zones reach that rule
with both coverage values missing (imputation comes after the rule): predict that every one of their
rural zone-years will go, Tunja's `{python} NUM[tj_rural0]` among them, along with every other zone-year
missing both coverages, while Tunja's urban zone, which takes the municipal total, stays. Then rebuild,
and check. `pre-render` re-runs the analysis and `freeze: false` re-executes every page. The kept rows
fall from `{python} w.fmt(len(c0))` to `{python} w.fmt(len(c1))`: the capitals'
`{python} w.fmt(len(cap0))` rural zone-years and `{python} w.fmt(other_both)` other zone-years missing
both coverages, and nothing else; Tunja's urban zone stays in cluster `{python} tj_c` in every year. k
stays `{python} after["k"]`, so the post's `assert k == 4` passes, the names stay, and
`{python} f"{same:.0%}"` of the remaining rows keep their cluster. The officials' report, the council's
slides, the post and the dashboard all change together, because none of them computes anything; the live
site does not change at all until you publish again.

That one exercise holds the part's design: one script, every publication reading its `outputs/`,
`pre-render` and `freeze: false` keeping both fresh (`freeze: auto` is faster, but needs a written rule for
clearing its cache), and guards that turn a silent inconsistency into a failed render. It is also the
book's method at full size, and the afterword takes it back to its three verbs, and to a project of your
own.
